title: DRS Just Bought the Army's AI Brain. Here's Why That's a Moat.
subtitle: Leonardo DRS is the defense-electronics pure-play hiding inside nearly every major U.S. weapon system — and its $450M grab of mission-software firm Raft just made it the AI layer of the Army's next-gen command network. Shares pulled back this week on headline noise; the structural story says that's a gift.
summary: Leonardo DRS makes the electro-optical sensors, electronic-warfare systems, tactical radars, and naval power gear inside nearly every major U.S. weapon system — the sensing-and-computing layer that AI-enabled warfare runs on. Its $450M acquisition of mission-software firm Raft plugs an AI brain into the Army's Next Generation Command and Control network, stacking on top of an 18-quarter book-to-bill streak, record funded backlog, and a net-cash balance sheet. Shares pulled back this week on Iran de-escalation headlines, but the structural story — software-defined warfare, sole-source programs, and an installed base that keeps getting paid to get smarter — is very much intact.

bodyHtml:
Here's a sentence you don't hear every day: the U.S. Army just effectively bought its AI brain for $450 million. That's the deal Leonardo DRS quietly announced at the end of July — a cash acquisition of Raft, a mission-software shop whose data and AI layer is being wired directly into the Army's next-generation command network. Think of it as the Pentagon's version of a cloud migration, and DRS just bought the company writing the middleware.

If you've never heard of Leonardo DRS, that's kind of the point. It's the defense-electronics pure-play that makes the electro-optical and infrared sensors, electronic-warfare systems, tactical radars, network computing, and naval power systems that go inside nearly every major U.S. weapon system. The Army, the Navy, allied militaries — they're all customers. And roughly 71% of the company sits with Italy's Leonardo S.p.A., making DRS the rare case of a European defense giant holding a majority stake in a U.S. defense pure-play.

Why does an electronics company matter to the AI story? Because warfare is going software-defined, fast. Sensors, autonomy, and AI are deciding fights faster than humans can — which means whoever owns the sensing-and-computing layer owns the whole stack. That's DRS's lane. It's not the flashy model maker; it's the shovel-seller, supplying the eyes, ears, and compute every AI-enabled system in the U.S. arsenal runs on.

The Raft deal is the tell. Raft builds the data and AI software layer for the Army's Next Generation Command and Control network — NGC2, the effort to replace a patchwork of legacy systems with one AI-native network. DRS isn't buying a chatbot. It's buying the connective tissue between every sensor it already builds and the commanders who need decisions in seconds.

Here's the moat: 18 straight quarters with book-to-bill at or above 1.0 — demand keeps outpacing delivery — plus a record funded backlog and long-cycle, sole-source programs. Columbia-class submarine propulsion? Sole source. A big chunk of the Navy's naval power business? Sole source. And much of its most important work is classified, which is its own kind of barrier to entry.

Competitors are real — L3Harris and Elbit in electro-optics, RTX and Anduril in electronic warfare and counter-drone. But DRS's edge is the installed base. Look at SGT STOUT, its mobile short-range air defense system: in a U.S. government test this month it took out Group 1 and 2 drone threats with a software upgrade — no new hardware. That's the whole thesis in one demo. Once your gear is in the field, you keep getting paid to make it smarter.

The catalysts keep stacking. Raft alone is doing heavy lifting: it won a $99 million Army enterprise contract in August to accelerate data and AI delivery, and it got picked for the Space Force's Kronos program. SGT STOUT's drone-killing test landed August 11. In February, DRS secured a role in the Missile Defense Agency's roughly $151 billion SHIELD program. In January it opened a new naval power and propulsion facility in South Carolina for Columbia-class work. Even Space42 — the UAE's AI-powered space venture — signed an MoU to bolt DRS mission systems onto its secure satellite connectivity for sovereign national security.

The financials back the story: adjusted EBITDA grew about 33% year over year in Q2, and management raised full-year guidance — again. The balance sheet is net cash, revenue has climbed from $2.83 billion in fiscal 2023 to roughly $3.65 billion last year, and there's a small dividend for people who like getting paid to wait. New CEO John Baylouny took the reins in January with a software-forward message.

Sure, shares pulled back this week — defense stocks broadly wobbled on Iran de-escalation headlines. That's noise, not thesis. The structural story is that every major military is spending like there's no tomorrow on sensors, networks, and AI, and DRS sits at the intersection of all three.

Bottom line: DRS is one of the cleanest ways to play software-defined warfare without chasing a meme. Majority-owned by a European giant, net cash on the books, an 18-quarter book-to-bill streak, an installed base that compounds, and now an actual AI software brain bolted on. The analysts see it too — consensus is Strong Buy, with a target mean well above where shares trade. Long cycle, deep moat, AI upside. That's a thesis worth more than a week of headlines.
